paragraphs: A clustering method can find the best partition of a dataset without recovering the structure that generated those observations. This paper makes that distinction central. When the observed data are a sample from a larger space, the statistical goal is to approximate a partition of that space. The authors argue that unrestricted optimization over sample partitions usually does not accomplish this.

Their alternative, nearest neighbor clustering, restricts the partitions considered to a particular class of functions. This changes the search problem: success is no longer defined solely by choosing the highest-scoring partition among every possible arrangement of the observed points. The restriction becomes part of how the method connects finite observations to an underlying population.

Using statistical learning theory, the authors prove statistical consistency for this approach. They also establish polynomial worst-case computational complexity by construction and describe a branch-and-bound implementation with low average-case complexity. The contribution therefore connects a statistical objective with computational design: restricting the search can support both meaningful recovery and manageable computation.
neurips-2007-consistent-minimization-of-.tldr: Restricting the clustering search yields a statistically consistent method with polynomial worst-case complexity.

paragraphs: Cascade detectors save computation by rejecting examples before every part of a classifier has been evaluated. Training them raises a difficult question: how much rejection should each stage perform? This paper proposes multiple-instance pruning, or MIP, to set thresholds automatically for soft cascades, avoiding the need to choose intermediate detection targets by hand.

The method combines two observations. An example that the complete classifier will ultimately reject can potentially be discarded earlier without changing that final decision. Also, face detection can be treated as a multiple-instance learning problem. Together, these ideas guide threshold selection toward earlier termination while preserving the relevant training-set outcomes.

The stated guarantee is specifically about the training dataset: the selected thresholds do not lower detection rate or raise false-positive rate there. MIP requires neither assumed probability distributions nor statistical independence. Experiments on the MIT+CMU dataset show significant performance advantages. The practical contribution is an automatic way to reduce cascade computation while explicitly protecting the training behavior of the complete detector.
neurips-2007-multiple-instance-pruning-f.tldr: MIP automatically prunes soft-cascade computation while preserving detection and false-positive rates on the training data.

paragraphs: Ranking data need not specify a complete ordering of every item. Different observations may provide different kinds of partial orderings, creating a challenge for combining them into one statistical model. This paper addresses that challenge when the number of items is large, a setting in which existing models of full and partial rankings can become computationally impractical.

The authors investigate nonparametric models and derive efficient procedures for working with partially ranked observations. Their derivations use combinatorial and algebraic properties of the lattice of partial rankings. This mathematical structure organizes relationships among partial rankings and supplies the basis for manipulating them without relying on computationally prohibitive conventional approaches.

The central result is a model that can efficiently aggregate different types of partial ranking data while satisfying coherence and consistency. The authors identify this combination as a first for nonparametric ranking models. Its significance lies in treating heterogeneous incomplete rankings within a common statistical framework while making computation feasible for larger collections of items.
neurips-2007-non-parametric-modeling-of-.tldr: A nonparametric framework efficiently combines different kinds of partial rankings into a coherent, consistent model.

paragraphs: Average learning curves can conceal how individual subjects actually learn. The paper starts from a reanalysis of classical conditioning in which individuals change their predictions abruptly and continue fluctuating, even though group averages suggest smooth learning toward a stable level. This creates a challenge for interpretations that directly associate smooth behavioral change with gradual Bayesian belief updating.

The authors propose that individuals approximate inference using sequential Monte Carlo sampling with very few samples. Their simulations use just one. Rather than maintaining a detailed representation of uncertainty across trials, an individual can operate with an extremely limited sampled representation, producing sudden and unstable changes in behavior.

When behavior is averaged across individuals, those separate samples collectively resemble the many samples used in a particle filter. The resulting group behavior can therefore resemble exact Bayesian inference. The model can also produce retrospective revaluation at the ensemble level. Its main implication is that sophisticated aggregate behavior can arise from much simpler individual inference processes than the average learning curve might suggest.
neurips-2007-the-rat-as-particle-filter-.tldr: A one-sample inference model explains how abrupt individual learning can produce smooth, Bayesian-looking group behavior.

paragraphs: Inferring a nonlinear dynamical system from sparse, noisy observations is difficult both statistically and computationally. The likelihood can have a complicated nonlinear shape, and evaluating candidate parameters can require explicitly solving the system. This paper introduces an accelerated sampling procedure for Bayesian parameter inference in both ordinary differential equations and equations involving time delays.

The method first applies Gaussian process regression to the observed time series. The fitted process supplies estimates of derivatives and time-delayed quantities that can be used for parameter inference. These estimates make it possible to work with the differential relationships without explicitly solving the dynamical system during the inference procedure.

The authors report dramatic computational savings and demonstrate speed and statistical accuracy on examples from both equation classes. They also compare the approach with contemporary methods. The key contribution is the use of a fitted statistical description of the observations to bypass costly system solutions, making Bayesian analysis of nonlinear dynamics more computationally accessible in the demonstrated settings.
neurips-2008-accelerating-bayesian-infer.tldr: Gaussian process estimates enable faster Bayesian inference for nonlinear differential equations without explicitly solving the dynamical system.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether supervised learning for mRNA splicing can benefit from transferring information between organisms. The central issue is domain transfer: a classification method must make use of information associated with one organism in a setting associated with another. The authors examine that issue using genomic sequence data rather than treating transfer as an abstract learning problem.

The study evaluates several domain adaptation approaches, including recent methods and some novel ones. It considers model organisms separated by different evolutionary distances. This makes relatedness an explicit part of the empirical comparison and lets the analysis examine transfer across biological settings that differ in how closely their organisms are related.

The reported finding is conditional: domain adaptation can improve classification when the organisms are not closely related. This supports its usefulness in those evaluated transfer settings without asserting that every adaptation method helps every organism pair. The contribution is empirical evidence connecting adaptation methods, evolutionary relatedness, and performance on a specific genomic classification task.
neurips-2008-an-empirical-analysis-of-do.tldr: Experiments show that domain adaptation can improve mRNA-splicing classification when transferring between organisms that are not closely related.

paragraphs: Learning depends on how sensory information is represented. Before a person or algorithm can use relevant features, those features must somehow be formed from the input. This paper treats that formation process as a learning problem in its own right, asking how people separate or combine elementary sensory components into useful representations.

The authors construct a rational model using nonparametric Bayesian statistics. It forms features directly from raw sensory data without requiring the number of features to be specified beforehand. That flexibility matters because the representation itself is something to infer, rather than a fixed set of ingredients supplied before learning begins.

The analysis compares how the model and human perception use two sources of information: patterns in the sensory observations and information about categories. The purpose is to identify influences on feature formation by examining their roles in both systems. The contribution is a framework for studying how representations emerge, with the comparison directed toward understanding the forces shaping human feature learning.
neurips-2008-analyzing-human-feature-lea.tldr: A nonparametric Bayesian model studies how people infer sensory features without a predetermined number of features.

paragraphs: Learning topic models from large text collections can demand substantial computation and memory. This paper distributes that work across processors for two unsupervised modeling frameworks: Latent Dirichlet Allocation and Hierarchical Dirichlet Processes. The goal is to learn a shared global topic model while allowing processors to carry out much of the inference independently.

Each processor runs Gibbs sampling on its own portion of the data and exchanges information with other processors through local asynchronous communication. This organization allows learning to proceed without making every exchange part of a single synchronized update. The paper also introduces a parallel HDP sampler as an intermediate step toward the asynchronous HDP method.

The experiments show global models with statistical accuracy comparable to standard LDA and HDP samplers, alongside significant improvements in time and memory. Speedup is demonstrated on a corpus containing 730 million words using 32 processors, with perplexity results extending to 1,500 virtual processors. These results support asynchronous communication as a practical approach to scaling topic-model inference.
neurips-2008-asynchronous-distributed-le.tldr: Asynchronous distributed sampling scales LDA and HDP learning while maintaining statistical accuracy comparable to standard samplers in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: A discount factor controls how strongly a decision-making algorithm values later rewards. It also helps ensure convergence in many methods for Markov decision processes, even when discounting has no intrinsic motivation in the task. This paper studies an intriguing consequence: deliberately lowering the discount factor can substantially improve approximate dynamic programming on some problems, including Tetris.

The authors first examine the usual bounds on approximation error. Those bounds can become smaller when the discount factor decreases, providing one explanation for the improvement. However, the paper also shows that these bounds are loose. A reduction in a loose bound does not by itself fully explain the observed practical benefit.

A second analysis focuses on problems in which rewards arrive only occasionally. For this setting, the authors derive tighter bounds that support substantial improvement from lower discounting. The resulting argument is conditional on the reward structure and approximation setting. It explains why changing the effective planning horizon can help on some tasks without claiming that lower discount factors always improve decisions.
neurips-2008-biasing-approximate-dynamic.tldr: Lower discount factors can improve approximate dynamic programming on some tasks, with tighter error bounds explaining benefits when rewards are sporadic.

paragraphs: An informative neural experiment depends on choosing stimuli that reveal the unknown properties of a receptive field. This paper improves stimulus selection by incorporating stronger prior knowledge about the field's possible form. Instead of using only broad expectations such as smoothness or sparsity, the method uses a parameterized model to direct experimental effort.

For example, if a Gabor function is believed to approximate the receptive field, the procedure selects stimuli to constrain quantities such as orientation and spatial frequency with as few trials as possible. The broader formulation assumes that plausible receptive fields lie near a known lower-dimensional surface within the full parameter space.

The method then targets uncertainty along the local tangent space of that surface, concentrating measurement on variations associated with the assumed model. Applications to simulated and real data indicate that this strategy may improve efficiency in many cases. The significance is that structured prior knowledge can guide which uncertainties an experiment resolves, with the reported gains remaining qualified rather than universal.
neurips-2008-designing-neurophysiology-e.tldr: Parameterized receptive-field priors guide stimulus selection to reduce relevant uncertainty and may make neural experiments more efficient.

paragraphs: Contours describe object shape compactly, but individual contours cover less spatial extent than region segments. This paper uses a second, related image to help determine which contours in the first image belong together. The guiding idea is that contours linked to their counterparts by similar transformations are likely to form a common group.

The method extracts visually salient contours and proposes transformations that align subsets across the images. For each transformation, shape matches identify groups that supply context for evaluating matches between individual contour points. Those contexts then support a final step that jointly groups contours in the original image and finds their counterparts in the related one.

Because matching relies on shape, the same approach applies to stereo pairs, motion pairs, and similar images without separate matching procedures for each setting. The authors demonstrate all three types of grouping and report qualitatively better results than a baseline without the inferred contexts. The findings support using cross-image relationships to enrich the evidence available for grouping individual contours.
neurips-2008-grouping-contours-via-a-rel.tldr: Shape correspondences with a related image provide context that improves contour grouping across stereo, motion, and similarity settings.

paragraphs: Bayesian decision-making provides a way to act under uncertainty, but its mathematical representations can be difficult to implement in neural networks. This paper asks whether a simple, biologically supported form of synaptic change could nevertheless learn optimal Bayesian decisions. Its proposed construction combines Hebbian learning with a sparse and redundant neural representation.

The authors give a concrete learning rule that operates on log-probability ratios. This connects synaptic adaptation to the quantities used in probabilistic decisions. Their central result is an in-principle demonstration: with the specified representation and learning mechanism, simple plasticity can support learning to make Bayesian-optimal choices.

The rule can also be modulated by reward signals, providing a possible account of how Bayesian inference supports rapid reinforcement learning in the brain. The authors show that it can model previously reported primate experiments on learning probabilistic inference. The contribution is a concrete connection between neural plasticity and probabilistic decision-making, while retaining the distinction between a possible mechanism and proof of the mechanism used by the brain.
neurips-2008-hebbian-learning-of-bayes-o.tldr: Hebbian plasticity with a sparse, redundant neural code can in principle learn Bayesian-optimal decisions and model reward-guided probabilistic learning.

paragraphs: Graph clustering often begins with data that are not already a graph. Similarities or distances between observations must first be converted into connections. This paper investigates whether that preliminary construction changes what the clustering method does. It focuses on criteria such as normalized cut, which can be applied to several different kinds of neighborhood graph.

The authors analyze what these criteria approach as the sample size grows. They find different limiting expressions for different graph constructions, including radius-based neighborhood graphs and nearest-neighbor graphs. Consequently, applying the same normalized-cut criterion to these graphs can lead to systematically different clustering behavior even in the large-sample limit.

The distinction also appears in examples using toy and real data with relatively small samples. Graph construction therefore affects more than a finite-sample implementation detail: it helps determine the effective clustering objective. The paper's central implication is that understanding or comparing a graph clustering criterion requires considering the type of graph on which that criterion is evaluated.
neurips-2008-influence-of-graph-construc.tldr: The same graph clustering criterion can have systematically different behavior depending on how the neighborhood graph is constructed.

paragraphs: Change-point analysis asks whether a sequence's observations switch from one distribution to another and, if so, when that switch occurs. This paper proposes a kernel-based method that addresses both questions using unlabeled temporal data. Its test statistic uses the maximum kernel Fisher discriminant ratio to assess differences between candidate segments.

The authors derive the statistic's limiting distribution when no change is present. They also establish consistency when a change does occur. These results support a hypothesis test with a prescribed false-alarm probability and a probability of detecting a change that approaches one as the sample size grows. The latter guarantee is explicitly a large-sample result.

When there is a distributional change, the same statistic supplies an estimate of its location. The authors present promising experiments on segmenting mental tasks from brain-computer-interface data and indexing pop songs. The contribution joins detection and localization in one statistical framework, with theory describing its asymptotic behavior and experiments illustrating its use on temporal segmentation problems.
neurips-2008-kernel-change-point-analysi.tldr: A kernel-based statistic detects and locates distribution changes, with false-alarm calibration and large-sample consistency.

paragraphs: Learning a Bayesian network involves balancing expressive structure against the cost of inference. Bounding treewidth helps keep inference tractable, but learning within that restriction can be difficult. The paper highlights that the fully greedy thin-junction-tree approach can overfit, especially with limited data, and proposes learning through more global changes to network structure.

The method maintains a triangulated graph and updates it dynamically to permit the addition of chain structures. These additions increase the treewidth bound by at most one. The resulting learning procedure is polynomial in both graph size and the treewidth bound, combining controlled structural growth with a computationally manageable search procedure.

Experiments on several real datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the method. The authors also report better generalization from global operators when learning networks without a treewidth restriction. That additional finding suggests that the benefit of their structural changes extends beyond enforcing tractable inference: the way the search modifies a network can also improve the learned model's generalization in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2008-learning-bounded-treewidth-.tldr: Global structural updates enable efficient learning of bounded-treewidth Bayesian networks and improve generalization in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Selective sampling lets a classifier request labels for only some observations. This paper analyzes an efficient margin-based algorithm to understand the tradeoff between reducing label use and approaching the best achievable prediction risk. The analysis covers both the selective version and a fully supervised version that receives every label.

The guarantees use the Tsybakov low-noise condition, whose positive exponent alpha characterizes the instance distribution. Ignoring logarithmic factors, the selective sampler's average risk approaches Bayes risk at rate n^{-(1+alpha)/(3+alpha)}, with labels sampled at the same rate. The fully supervised algorithm achieves the faster rate n^{-(1+alpha)/(2+alpha)} while using all labels.

These results quantify a conditional tradeoff: selective sampling reduces labeling while giving up some convergence speed as a function of the number of observations. The paper also tests simple variants on text data, where they perform much better than popular competitors of similar computational efficiency. The contribution combines noise-dependent theoretical guarantees with empirical evidence that inexpensive selective methods can be practically effective.
neurips-2008-linear-classification-and-s.tldr: Low-noise analysis quantifies how an efficient selective classifier trades fewer labels for slower risk convergence than full supervision.

paragraphs: Real-time model learning requires both updating a predictor and answering queries quickly. The paper considers settings such as learning inverse robot dynamics for model-based control, where regression must keep pace with ongoing operation. It proposes accelerating Gaussian process regression by replacing one global model with a collection of local Gaussian process models.

Training observations are divided into local regions, and each region receives its own model. To predict at a query point, the method combines estimates from nearby models using weights. Distance determines both how the data are partitioned and how local predictions are combined, giving the approach a common organizing principle for learning and prediction.

The authors report real-time online learning and prediction. In comparisons with other nonparametric regression methods, local Gaussian processes are more accurate than LWPR and close to standard Gaussian process regression and nu-SVR. The findings support local modeling as a way to retain much of the predictive performance of the compared methods while meeting the speed requirements of the demonstrated online setting.
neurips-2008-local-gaussian-process-regr.tldr: Distance-based local Gaussian processes provide real-time online regression with accuracy close to standard Gaussian process regression in the reported comparisons.

paragraphs: An optimal policy for a Markov decision process supplies a prescription for decision-making. That can be sufficient when a machine executes the policy, but human decision support may benefit from offering flexibility among good choices. This paper asks how to represent and find near-optimal policies that leave room for the person making the decisions.

The authors introduce non-deterministic MDP policies to address this goal. The motivation is to make multiple acceptable choices available while retaining a near-optimality requirement. This changes the planning question from merely finding an optimal prescription to identifying a more flexible policy whose permitted choices remain tied to the quality of the resulting decisions.

Two computational solutions are proposed: one based on mixed-integer programming and another on search. The paper includes experiments applying the framework to treatment-choice optimization in a medical decision support system. Its contribution is a formal and algorithmic approach to flexibility in sequential decisions, illustrated through that application rather than a claim that the framework establishes clinical benefits.
neurips-2008-mdps-with-non-deterministic.tldr: Non-deterministic MDP policies offer flexibility among near-optimal choices, with proposed mixed-integer-programming and search methods.

paragraphs: People learn relationships between continuous quantities, but explanations of this ability have often emphasized two different mechanisms. One says that learners infer an explicit function or rule. The other says that they associate observations through similarity. This paper develops a rational analysis that places these perspectives within a common account of function learning.

The mathematical connection comes from the equivalence between Bayesian linear regression and Gaussian processes. Under that connection, a description in terms of explicit functions and a description in terms of similarity can express the same solution. The distinction between the two accounts therefore need not imply fundamentally separate approaches to the learning problem.

Using this insight, the authors define a Gaussian process model intended to combine the strengths of both perspectives. Its importance is conceptual as well as computational: it provides a shared framework for discussing rule-based and similarity-based learning. The stated contribution is the construction of this unified model, connecting ideas from statistical regression to the question of how humans learn functional relationships.
neurips-2008-modeling-human-function-lea.tldr: A Gaussian process account unifies explicit-rule and similarity-based views of human function learning.

paragraphs: Estimating a joint distribution over many binary variables becomes expensive because the representation can grow exponentially. With d variables, the orthogonal expansion considered here contains 2^d coefficients. This paper develops a recursive estimator that makes the problem more manageable for a broad class of distributions satisfying a specified sparsity condition.

The estimator adapts to sparsity without requiring its level to be known in advance. Statistically, it achieves mean-squared error close to the minimax benchmark, which describes the best worst-case performance for the relevant class. Computationally, sparser distributions require less work. Thus the same structural property supports both estimation quality and reduced computation.

Under the stated sparsity condition, the procedure runs in probabilistic polynomial time rather than incurring the conventional exponential burden. It also allows flexible control over the balance between mean-squared error and computational cost. The contribution is therefore a conditional way around a large representation: recursive estimation exploits sparsity while allowing the user to trade additional computation for statistical accuracy.
neurips-2008-near-minimax-recursive-dens.tldr: A recursive estimator exploits unknown sparsity to achieve near-minimax accuracy with probabilistic polynomial computation for suitable binary distributions.

paragraphs: Classification algorithms often optimize a surrogate loss in place of classification error itself. Classification calibration connects minimizing that surrogate to minimizing classification risk, but it does not by itself provide an efficient optimization algorithm. This paper addresses that algorithmic question for a broad class of calibrated losses.

The proposed method provably minimizes classification-calibrated surrogates that are strictly convex and differentiable. This class includes exponential, logistic, and squared losses. Its convergence guarantees are of a boosting type and depend on a weak learning assumption. These conditions matter because the optimization claim applies to the specified loss family and learning setting.

The authors also identify balanced convex surrogates, a subclass connected to maximum-likelihood estimation, zero-sum games, and common requirements for supervised losses. Experiments examine 11 variants of the algorithm across more than 50 domains. They explore new surrogates and the potential of tuning losses to the data, complementing the theoretical result with an investigation of how different loss choices behave in practice.
neurips-2008-on-the-efficient-minimizati.tldr: A boosting-style algorithm provably minimizes a broad class of calibrated losses under a weak learning assumption.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes a kernel classifier whose objective is the integrated squared error of a difference between densities. Like a support vector machine, it is obtained by solving a quadratic program and produces a sparse classifier. A distinguishing feature is that the formulation does not involve a regularization parameter.

The authors establish a distribution-free concentration inequality for a cross-validation estimate of integrated squared error. Such a result controls how the estimated error relates to its statistical target. They use this foundation to derive an oracle inequality and prove consistency for both the density-difference error criterion and the probability of misclassification.

These guarantees connect the quantity optimized by the method to the prediction behavior ultimately of interest. The analysis therefore goes beyond the classifier's computational resemblance to an SVM and supplies a statistical basis for evaluating it. The results can also be specialized to an existing L2 kernel density estimator, extending their relevance from classification to the related task of estimating a density.
neurips-2008-performance-analysis-for-l-.tldr: Statistical guarantees establish consistency of an L2 kernel classifier in both integrated squared error and misclassification probability.

paragraphs: Ranking is a structured prediction problem because an object's position depends on its relationship to other objects. An error involving one item can affect the correctness of several other ordering decisions. This paper addresses how to represent those dependencies probabilistically when the number of objects makes general structured prediction difficult.

The proposed framework uses cumulative distribution networks to model joint cumulative distribution functions over multiple pairwise preferences. Rather than treating every preference as isolated, it represents their collective structure. This supplies a graphical modeling approach for expressing dependencies that matter to the quality of an overall ranking.

The authors apply the framework to document retrieval on OHSUMED and show that RankNet, ListNet, and ListMLE can be interpreted as particular instances of cumulative distribution networks. That connection places several existing probabilistic ranking models within a shared framework. The stated contribution also includes opening a broader class of flexible structured loss functions for exploration, expanding the ways a learning algorithm can represent and penalize ranking errors.
neurips-2008-structured-ranking-learning.tldr: Cumulative distribution networks model dependent ranking preferences and unify several existing probabilistic ranking methods.

paragraphs: Transfer learning becomes especially challenging when source and target data use entirely different features. This paper proposes translated learning to move useful label information across that divide. Its motivating example is using labeled text to help classify images when labeled images are difficult to obtain.

The method builds a sequence of connections between the two spaces. A language model first relates class labels to source features. A translator connects those source features to target features, and the chain then reaches the target instances. The authors express this linked pathway using a Markov chain and risk minimization, turning cross-space transfer into a statistical learning framework.

Experiments cover text-assisted image classification and classification across languages. In these tasks, the authors report that translated learning can substantially outperform many leading baseline methods. The important idea is that knowledge transfer can proceed through explicit intermediate links even when the source and target do not share a feature representation. The empirical claim concerns the tested tasks rather than every possible pair of learning spaces.
neurips-2008-translated-learning-transfe.tldr: Translated learning transfers label information across different feature spaces through a probabilistic chain linking labels, features, and target instances.

paragraphs: Adapting to a changed visual environment involves both adjusting movements and changing where sensory cues seem to be located. Earlier models treated sensory adaptation as a response to disagreement between visual and proprioceptive hand-position estimates, separate from motor adaptation. This paper proposes a unified explanation for both components.

The model uses optimal Bayesian estimation to assign perceived errors to sensory and motor contributions. Both forms of adaptation emerge from this shared estimation process. The authors show that the model accounts for patterns of movement errors during visuomotor adaptation as well as the perceptual aftereffects that remain afterward.

The shared mechanism produces a further prediction: adapting to a force field should also shift perception, even when visual and proprioceptive observations never disagree. The authors test and confirm this prediction experimentally. This result matters because it supports a route to sensory change beyond direct disagreement between the two senses, connecting perceptual adaptation to how the system interprets the sources of errors during action.
neurips-2008-unifying-the-sensory-and-mo.tldr: A unified Bayesian model links sensory and motor adaptation and correctly predicts perceptual shifts following force-field adaptation.
